message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  It is commonly quoted as the **Shannon number**, named after Claude Shannon, who first estimated it in 1950.

> **Shannon number ≈ 10^43**  
> (more precisely, about 10^43 to 10^50 depending on the assumptions used)

This figure comes from a rough combinatorial analysis of all the ways pieces can be arranged on the board, respecting the rules of movement, capture, castling, en‑passant, promotion, and the constraints on the number of each piece type.  Modern computational studies refine this estimate, but the consensus remains that the number of legal positions is on the order of 10^43.

For comparison, the total number of possible games (sequences of moves) is even larger—roughly 10^120.  But when people ask “how many possible arrangements” they almost always mean the number of distinct board positions, which is about 10^43.
